In prophetic theology, arrogance (*al-kibr*) is the most abhorrent sin before God, because greatness (*al-kibriyāʾ*) is a garment that belongs exclusively to the Creator. In a profound *ḥadīth qudsī*, God declares: *“Grandeur is My cloak, and majesty is My garment; whoever competes with Me in either of them, I will cast him into the Fire”* (*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2620*).

The Prophet ﷺ detailed the ultimate humiliation awaiting the proud on the Day of Resurrection: *“The arrogant will be gathered on the Day of Resurrection like tiny ants in the form of men; humiliation will overcome them from every place, until they are driven into a prison in Hell called Būlas, overwhelmed by the fire of fires”* (*Sunan al-Tirmidhī 2492, graded ḥasan*). Those who inflated their egos in this world, walking with haughty steps and looking down upon truth and humanity, will be reduced to the smallest, most despised creatures on the Day of Account.

**The Urgent Call to Cultivate Humility**

Verse 39:60 stands as a severe warning against every form of arrogance—intellectual, social, financial, or spiritual. When an individual feels superior to others, mocks divine commandments, or refuses to admit error, they are cultivating the seeds that will bloom into a blackened face on the Day of Judgment.

The antidote is the radical cultivation of humility (*tawāḍuʿ*). The Prophet ﷺ promised: *“No one humbles himself for the sake of Allah except that Allah elevates him”* (*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2588*). Lowering one's forehead to the dust in sincere prostration purifies the soul of arrogance, illuminating the inner mirror of the heart. By walking through mortal life with humble reverence, the believer ensures that when the great trumpet sounds, their face will emerge radiant, joyful, and enveloped in the welcoming light of the Lord of the worlds. That radiant illumination is the eternal crown of those who lived for divine truth alone. In that blessed light, every humble soul finds everlasting honor and peace.
verses.61:
> And Allah will deliver those who were mindful ˹of Him˺ to their place of ˹ultimate˺ triumph. No evil will touch them, nor will they grieve

**The Divine Rescue of the Reverent**

The discourse pivots with radiant majesty from the blackened faces and eternal imprisonment of the arrogant in verse 60 to the triumphant deliverance of the faithful: *wa-yunajjī Allāhu alladhīna ittaqaw bi-mafāzatihim* ("And Allah will deliver those who were mindful of Him to their place of ultimate triumph"). The verb *yunajjī* (second verbal form) signifies deliberate, complete, and active rescue from the midst of mortal danger. The righteous are not left to stumble through the terrifying landscapes of the Resurrection on their own strength; God Himself intervenes to extract and protect them.

The noun *mafāzah* derives from the root *f-w-z*, meaning triumph, ultimate success, deliverance, and entering into safety. In classical Arabic semantics, a desert crossing or safe haven is poetically called a *mafāzah* as an omen of safe arrival. Here, it denotes their supreme victory: attaining salvation from the Fire and entering the gardens of Paradise. The prepositional construct *bi-mafāzatihim* ("by/to their place of triumph") indicates that their rescue is intimately linked to the righteous deeds, mindful reverence (*taqwā*), and sincere monotheism they cultivated during earthly life.

**Absolute Immunity From Physical and Spiritual Evil**

The divine guarantee is articulated through an unshakeable negative: *lā yamassuhumu al-sūʾ* ("No evil will touch them"). The verb *yamassu* denotes the slightest graze, brush, or contact. While the deniers in verse 24 were depicted desperately shielding their faces from the awful punishment, the mindful believers are granted such absolute immunity that not a single spark of heat, a whisper of terror, or an atom of harm will come into physical contact with them.

In Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ, the Qur'an paints this serene sanctuary: *“They will not hear the slightest sound of it, and they will abide eternally in that which their souls desire”* (21:102). Even as the cosmic bridge spans the abyss and the cries of the condemned echo across the plains of reckoning, the reverent walk in complete, tranquil security, surrounded by angels of mercy who welcome them into celestial peace.

**The Permanent Extinction of Grief**

The second dimension of their protection addresses internal emotional consciousness: *wa-lā hum yaḥzanūn* ("nor will they grieve"). In human experience, relief from physical danger does not automatically guarantee happiness; an individual may escape an accident yet remain shattered by grief over lost loved ones, wasted opportunities, or traumatic memories. The Qur'an guarantees that for the dwellers of the Garden, psychological sorrow (*al-ḥuzn*) is permanently eradicated.

They will feel no grief over the earthly life they left behind, because its transient pleasures pale into insignificance before the radiant reality of Paradise. Nor will they grieve over their future, because their bliss is eternal, guarded by a divine promise that never fails (*39:20*). As the people of the Garden proclaim upon crossing the celestial gates: *“Praise be to Allah, who has removed from us all sorrow; indeed, our Lord is Forgiving and Appreciative”* (35:34). Sorrow is an emotion belonging exclusively to the mortal trial; in the presence of the Lord, only joy endures.

**The Ultimate Meaning of Fawz in Scripture**

The concept of *al-fawz* (triumph) represents the supreme summit of human ambition in the Qur'anic worldview. The Qur'an systematically qualifies this term across chapters: *al-fawz al-ʿaẓīm* (the magnificent triumph, 4:13), *al-fawz al-mubīn* (the manifest triumph, 45:30), and *al-fawz al-kabīr* (the great triumph, 85:11). True victory is not defined by winning political elections, accumulating financial empires, or conquering foreign lands.

A person may conquer the entire globe yet arrive on the Day of Resurrection bankrupt, facing eternal disgrace. Conversely, an impoverished slave who died in chains while holding fast to monotheism attains *al-mafāzah*. True triumph is passing the only examination that cannot be repeated: emerging from the divine courtroom exonerated, entering the everlasting gardens, and being enveloped in the good pleasure of the Almighty (*9:72*).

**The Symmetry of Retribution and Salvation**

Verses 60 and 61 present the ultimate aesthetic and theological symmetry of Sūrah az-Zumar. In verse 60, we witness the faces of the proud liars blackened with humiliation, dragged into the prison of Hell. In verse 61, we behold the mindful servants rescued by divine hand, elevated to the heights of triumph, untouched by harm and strangers to grief.

This sharp juxtaposition forces the reader to make an existential choice. Every human life is an investment leading toward one of these two outcomes. The path of pride and polytheistic compromise leads to the blackened face and the fiery pit; the path of humble mindfulness and sincere devotion leads to the place of ultimate triumph. By placing both destinies side by side, the Qur'an strips away all middle ground, calling humanity to immediate moral clarity.

**Cultivating Taqwā in the Present World**

The key that unlocks *al-mafāzah* is explicitly named as *taqwā*—mindful reverence of God. *Taqwā* is not an elusive mystical state; it is practical moral discipline cultivated in daily choices. It is restraining the eyes from forbidden sights, guarding the tongue from slander, dealing honestly in commerce, and maintaining devotion when alone in the dark.

The Prophet ﷺ summarized this path when asked about what most frequently admits people into Paradise, replying: *“Mindfulness of Allah (taqwā Allāh) and good character”* (*Sunan al-Tirmidhī 2004, graded ḥasan*). By making *taqwā* the foundation of their lives, the faithful build an invisible shield that protects their hearts in this world and guarantees their triumphant deliverance on the Day of Resurrection, securing an eternal inheritance where no evil touches them and grief is forgotten forever. Walking in daily obedience transforms ordinary human actions into steps leading directly to eternal felicity. In that constant vigilance, the servant finds everlasting tranquility and divine shelter.
verses.62:
> Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the Maintainer of everything

**The Absolute Universal Scope of Divine Creation**

The discourse establishes the supreme metaphysical foundation of monotheism with breathtaking economy: *Allāhu khāliqu kulli shayʾ* ("Allah is the Creator of all things"). The nominal syntax places the supreme divine name *Allāh* as the absolute subject, identifying Him as the solitary Originator of the entire cosmos. In Arabic grammar, the universal quantifier *kulli shayʾ* ("every thing") encompasses every single entity that exists outside the uncreated divine essence. It is an absolute, unqualified statement of ontological supremacy that leaves no corner of existence unauthored.

Everything in existence—the galaxies, stellar clusters, subatomic particles, biological organisms, angelic hosts, human souls, and the temporal flow of time itself—is a created object (*makhlūq*). Nothing exists by chance, nothing emerged spontaneously from non-being, and no secondary force possesses autonomous creative power. Classical theologians, including al-Ashʿarī and al-Māturīdī, emphasized that this clause definitively refutes all dualistic and polytheistic systems: there is only one Creator, and all else is His creation. Creation is an unshared divine act that encompasses all realms of reality.

**The Sovereign Reality of Continuous Maintenance**

The second clause articulates the ongoing, active relationship between the Creator and the cosmos: *wa-huwa ʿalā kulli shayʾin wakīl* ("and He is the Maintainer / Guardian of everything"). The noun *wakīl* in Qur'anic usage denotes far more than an earthly legal agent; it signifies the supreme Custodian, Disposer of affairs, Sustainer, Guardian, and Trustee who continuously manages, preserves, and oversees every detail of creation.

The cosmos is not a wound-up clockwork mechanism that God created and then abandoned to run autonomously, as deistic philosophies imagine. Creation requires continuous divine intervention to remain in existence at every fraction of a second. If God were to withhold His sustaining power for the blink of an eye, the entire universe would instantly collapse into non-being. As Sūrah Fāṭir proclaims: *“Indeed, Allah holds the heavens and the earth, lest they cease. And if they should cease, no one could hold them after Him”* (35:41). Continuous preservation is the signature of living divine sovereignty.

**The Complete Demolition of Polytheistic Intermediaries**

By uniting absolute creation (*khalq*) with absolute custodianship (*wikālah*), verse 39:62 completely annihilates the rationale behind polytheism. The pagan Arabs acknowledged that God was the supreme Creator (*39:38*), yet they justified worshipping secondary deities by claiming that those intermediaries managed localized affairs: rain, warfare, healing, fertility, and travel.

The verse shatters this functional polytheism. If God alone is the *Wakīl* over *everything*, then no stone idol, planetary angel, or deceased saint manages a single atom of the universe. There is no decentralized celestial bureaucracy, no division of cosmic labor, and no delegated spheres of divine authority. Every rain drop that falls, every leaf that flutters, and every heartbeat that pulses is directly maintained by the Lord of the worlds. To direct prayer, sacrifice, or supplication to created intermediaries is to worship an entity that is itself entirely dependent upon God for its continuous existence.

**The Radical Equality of All Created Beings**

This universal declaration establishes the radical ontological equality of all creation before the Creator. The highest archangel, the seal of the prophets, the microscopic bacterium, and the distant star all share the identical metaphysical status: they are created things (*kullu shayʾ*), entirely dependent upon the Maintainer.

No human being possesses inherent supremacy over another by virtue of race, tribe, or lineage. No created being can claim divine status, demand unquestioning worship, or lord over fellow mortals. Humanity stands as a single fraternity of servants before the solitary Lord. As the Prophet ﷺ declared in his Farewell Pilgrimage: *“O people, your Lord is One and your father is one. An Arab has no superiority over a non-Arab, nor has a non-Arab any superiority over an Arab; nor has a white person any superiority over a black person, nor a black person over a white person, except through piety (taqwā)”* (*Musnad Aḥmad 23489, graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Albānī*).

**The Spiritual Fortress of Absolute Tawakkul**

Knowing that God is the *Wakīl* over all things provides the ultimate foundation for spiritual reliance (*tawakkul*). When a believer internalizes that their health, livelihood, safety, and future are held in the hands of the omnipotent Maintainer of the universe, paralyzing anxieties evaporate. Human beings cannot control the future, and earthly patrons cannot guarantee security.

The believer acts with diligence, works honestly, and employs practical means, but their heart rests in serene trust upon the supreme *Wakīl*. As the Qur'an repeatedly commands the Messenger: *“And put your trust in the Living who does not die, and hymn His praise”* (25:58), and *“Allah is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs”* (3:173). In an unpredictable, turbulent world, resting upon the Maintainer of all things provides unbreakable peace and courage, freeing the human spirit from fear of future misfortune.

**The Direct Path of Unmediated Devotion**

The synthesis of creation and custodianship points the human soul directly toward its Maker. If God created you out of nothingness, sculpted you in the womb (*39:6*), provides your daily bread (*39:52*), and maintains your every breath, to whom else could your heart possibly turn?

Verse 39:62 sweeps away all theological clutter, leaving the soul standing directly before its Creator. Monotheism is not an abstract metaphysical theory; it is the natural, joyful recognition of reality. The verse summons every human being to align their internal worship with the objective structure of the universe: to worship the One who created all things, and to place their absolute reliance upon the One who maintains all that exists. In that pure alignment, the human spirit discovers its true purpose, dignity, and everlasting peace. Such unwavering devotion anchors the believer amidst every earthly storm.
verses.63:
> To Him belong the keys ˹of the treasuries˺ of the heavens and the earth. As for those who rejected the signs of Allah, it is they who will be the ˹true˺ losers

**The Celestial Sovereign of Cosmic Keys**

Following the declaration of creation and maintenance in verse 62, the discourse reveals the exclusive control of cosmic resources: *lahu maqālīdu al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ* ("To Him belong the keys of the treasuries of the heavens and the earth"). Placing the prepositional phrase *lahu* ahead of the subject creates grammatical restriction (*ḥaṣr*), establishing that these keys belong exclusively to God. Divine ownership is absolute, leaving no room for rival claimants or secondary administrators in the cosmic order.

The rare noun *maqālīd* is the plural of *miqlād* or *uqlīd*, an ancient Arabic term borrowed from Semitic cognates denoting a key, lock, storehouse mechanism, or bolt. In classical Arabic metaphor, possessing the "keys" (*al-maqālīd*) signifies having unrestricted authority, sovereign ownership, and complete administrative control over a house and its contents. To hold the keys of the heavens and the earth means that God alone opens and closes the celestial gates of mercy, rainfall, revelation, and angels, as well as the terrestrial gates of agriculture, mineral wealth, life, and mortality. No entity can challenge His absolute administrative monopoly.

**The Inexhaustible Celestial Treasuries**

Classical exegetes, such as al-Ṭabarī, al-Zamakhsharī, and al-Rāzī, explain that *maqālīd* refers to the keys of the divine treasuries (*khazāʾin*). This connects directly to the profound cosmological statement in Sūrah al-Ḥijr: *“And there is not a thing but that with Us are its depositories, and We do not send it down except according to a known measure”* (15:21), and Sūrah al-Munāfiqūn: *“And to Allah belong the depositories of the heavens and the earth, but the hypocrites do not understand”* (63:7).

Every blessing enjoyed by mortal creatures—physical nourishment, intellectual inspiration, spiritual peace, and technological discovery—is drawn from these celestial treasuries. God unlocks these depositories according to His infinite wisdom, measuring out portions suited to the spiritual welfare of His creatures (*39:52*). No emperor can force these gates open, and no economic monopoly can padlock them shut. The riches of the universe are distributed under sovereign care that never runs dry.

**The Spiritual Dimension: Keys to the Hearts**

Scholars of the inward life, including al-Tustarī, perceived a profound psychological and spiritual meaning within this verse. Beyond physical rain and material wealth, the most precious treasuries of the heavens and the earth are human hearts (*al-qulūb*). The key to spiritual guidance, faith, wisdom, and love belongs exclusively to the Almighty.

A scholar can deliver eloquent lectures, and a parent can offer compassionate advice, but neither holds the key to unlock a hardened heart. Only God opens the breast to Islam (*39:22*), and only God illuminates the inner eye with the light of revelation. The believer recognizes this total dependence, turning to the Holder of the keys in daily supplication, pleading for the keys of wisdom, patience, and steadfast devotion. Spiritual transformation is a divine gift unlocked by grace rather than human engineering.

**The Tragic Irony of Polytheistic Beggary**

Verse 39:63 exposes the hilarious, tragic absurdity of polytheism and secular materialism. The polytheists bowed down before stone idols, begging for rain, health, fertility, and victory in battle. Yet those idols possessed not a single key to any treasury. They were powerless beggars in God's universe.

As Sūrah Ṣād asks with biting sarcasm: *“Or do they have the depositories of the mercy of your Lord, the Exalted in Might, the Bestower?”* (38:9). To bypass the King who holds every key to the palace, and instead plead with an inanimate stone standing outside the gate, is the ultimate intellectual failure. Polytheism is a tragic diversion that cuts off the soul from the very Source of life. It trades infinite celestial abundance for imaginary phantoms that possess no reality or power.

**The Radical Definition of Ultimate Bankruptcy**

The second half of the verse pronounces the inescapable judicial verdict: *wa-alladhīna kafarū bi-āyāti Allāhi ulāʾika humu al-khāsirūn* ("As for those who rejected the signs of Allah, it is they who will be the true losers"). The demonstrative *ulāʾika*, reinforced by the isolating pronoun *hum*, creates absolute exclusivity: they, and they alone, are the ultimate losers.

In commercial societies like seventh-century Makkah, loss was measured in failed caravan investments or lost silver. The Qur'an radically redefines bankruptcy (*al-khusrān*). True loss is not financial hardship; it is rejecting the signs of the Creator who holds the keys of existence. By denying revelation, the denier padlocks themselves outside the treasuries of divine mercy. They lose their own souls, their families, and their eternal destiny (*39:15*), arriving on the Day of Resurrection with empty hands, facing an eternity of regret. That spiritual destitution is the only real catastrophe.

**The Serenity of Relying on the Key-Holder**

Knowing that the keys of the heavens and the earth belong to God provides the believer with unshakeable peace and freedom from human servitude. You no longer need to flatter tyrants, compromise your ethical principles, or live in terror of economic depression. The keys to your provision and survival are not in the hands of an employer, a government, or a hostile enemy; they are held by the Most Merciful Lord.

The believer acts with diligence, walks with dignity, and keeps their hands open in generous charity, knowing that the divine treasuries are inexhaustible. When a door of worldly opportunity closes, the soul does not fall into bitter despair; it turns to the Holder of all keys, confident that He will unlock a better, purer path leading to eternal felicity in the world to come. Resting in this assurance liberates human consciousness from anxiety and establishes a life anchored in unwavering gratitude and hope.
verses.64:
> Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Are you urging me to worship ˹anyone˺ other than Allah, O ignorant ones?”

**A Sharp Prophetic Repudiation of Idolatrous Proposals**

The discourse commands the Prophet to issue an uncompromising intellectual and moral confrontation: *qul a-fa-ghayra Allāhi taʾmurūnnī aʿbudu ayyuhā al-jāhilūn* ("Say, O Prophet, ‘Are you urging me to worship anyone other than Allah, O ignorant ones?’"). In Arabic rhetoric, the syntactic fronting of *a-fa-ghayra Allāh* ("Is it other than Allah?") combined with the interrogative hamzah conveys profound amazement, indignance, and absolute rejection (*istifhām al-inkār wa-l-taʿajjub*). It establishes an immediate boundary against polytheistic encroachment, clearing the ground of compromise.

The historical context illuminates the sharpness of this address. The pagan aristocracy of Makkah, exhausted by their failure to suppress the message through persecution, approached the Prophet with diplomatic compromises. They suggested syncretic arrangements: *“O Muḥammad, worship our gods for a year, and we will worship your God for a year; if what you bring is better, we partake in it, and if what we have is better, you partake in it.”* Verse 39:64 is the divine response commanded to the Prophet, blowing away their diplomatic negotiations with intellectual contempt, proving that divine truth cannot be divided or diluted.

**The Diagnostic Indictment of Jahl**

The verse addresses the polytheistic elite not with their cherished titles of nobility, tribal seniority, or commercial wealth, but with the stark diagnosis: *ayyuhā al-jāhilūn* ("O ignorant ones!"). In Qur'anic semantics, *al-jahl* is not merely the absence of basic literacy or speculative information. The leaders of the Quraysh were shrewd merchants, master orators, and skilled political strategists.

In sacred terminology, *al-jahl* is the failure of the intellect to act in accordance with objective moral and cosmic reality. It is spiritual foolishness, emotional volatility, and intellectual blindness that prefers inanimate stone to the uncreated Creator. To possess knowledge of trade routes and poetry while failing to recognize the Lord who holds the keys of the heavens and the earth (*39:63*) is the ultimate ignorance. The verse strips away their pretense of sophistication, exposing the primitive foolishness beneath their polite diplomatic proposals, reminding them that true intellect is verified by ethical obedience.

**The Absurdity of Exchanging Sovereignty for Impotence**

Verse 39:64 directly builds upon the cosmological declarations of verses 62 and 63. Having established that God alone created all things, that God alone maintains the cosmos, and that God alone holds the keys of all celestial and terrestrial treasuries, the proposal of the polytheists is revealed as breathtaking madness. Divine reality is singular, absolute, and unshared across every dimension of existence.

They were inviting the Messenger of God to abandon the uncreated Sovereign of the universe and bow his head before stone statues that created nothing, own nothing, and control nothing (*39:43*). It is the equivalent of demanding that a free prince abandon his palace and royal father to become the servant of an inanimate rock. The Prophet's rhetorical question exposes the monstrous intellectual regression inherent in polytheism: how can anyone possessing a sound intellect urge another to trade absolute perfection for absolute helplessness? It is a proposal born of profound spiritual blindness.

**The Inviolable Boundary of Monotheistic Integrity**

The verse establishes that monotheism (*tawḥīd*) cannot be subject to political negotiation, cultural compromise, or diplomatic appeasement. In worldly politics, compromise is often hailed as pragmatic wisdom: competing factions make mutual concessions to maintain social harmony and economic stability. Human legislation routinely balances competing interests through negotiation.

In the realm of ultimate theological truth, however, compromise is fatal treason. Truth cannot be blended with falsehood to achieve social peace. One cannot worship God on Fridays and Hubal on Saturdays. The confession of faith (*lā ilāha illā Allāh*) is an absolute demarcation line. By commanding the Prophet to call his own tribal elders *al-jāhilūn*, the Qur'an teaches that when fundamental moral and cosmic realities are at stake, clarity must supersede polite social accommodation. Standing upon uncompromised principle is the only foundation for enduring righteousness.

**The Courage of Uncompromising Witness**

Uttering this verse required extraordinary spiritual and physical courage from the Prophet ﷺ. In tribal Arabia, addressing powerful clan chieftains—men who possessed private militias, wealth, and fierce pride—as "ignorant ones" was an act of revolutionary defiance that invited assassination.

Yet the Prophet spoke the words without hesitation, fear, or flattery. He was anchored in the absolute sufficiency of his Lord (*39:36*). This uncompromising courage demonstrated the authenticity of his prophetic mission. A false prophet seeking personal power or social acceptance would have accepted the compromise, enjoying wealth and status as the head of a syncretic Arabian pantheon. The true Messenger of God chose persecution, boycott, and exile rather than compromise an atom of divine oneness. His fearless proclamation remains an inspiring beacon of spiritual integrity.

**A Universal Mandate for Moral Clarity**

Verse 39:64 stands as an eternal model for believers confronted by corrupt societal demands. In every age, prevailing cultures attempt to pressure the faithful into ideological syncretism, urging them to bow before contemporary secular idols: material consumerism, moral relativism, and hedonistic individualism. Society constantly whispers: *“Conform to our ways, dilute your sacred boundaries, and we will grant you social acceptance.”*

The believer responds with the prophetic clarity of this verse. When urged to compromise fundamental divine laws, the servant of God does not stutter in embarrassment; they stand firm upon revealed truth. True enlightenment is not following the shifting fads of human culture; it is submitting to the uncreated Sovereign of the cosmos. The verse calls every believer to maintain intellectual integrity, refusing to surrender sacred truth to the demands of spiritual ignorance. In that resolute fidelity, the human soul finds its true dignity, anchored in an unshakeable bond with the Lord of the worlds. That unwavering stand preserves the light of faith across generations.
verses.65:
> It has already been revealed to you—and to those ˹prophets˺ before you—that if you associate others ˹with Allah˺, your deeds will certainly be void and you will truly be one of the losers

**The Universal Prophetic Warning Against Shirk**

The discourse establishes the supreme constitutional law of divine revelation: *wa-laqad ūḥiya ilayka wa-ilā alladhīna min qablika la-in ashrakta la-yaḥbaṭanna ʿamaluka wa-la-takūnanna mina al-khāsirīn* ("It has already been revealed to you—and to those prophets before you—that if you associate others with Allah, your deeds will certainly be void and you will truly be one of the losers"). The particle sequence *wa-laqad ūḥiya* combines an oath with the particle of certainty, establishing that this is not a localized or temporary ruling, but the eternal, unalterable covenant binding every prophetic dispensation across human history.

From Adam, Noah, and Abraham to Moses, Jesus, and Muḥammad, every messenger received this identical warning. The conditional clause is addressed directly to the Prophet ﷺ in the singular: *la-in ashrakta* ("if you should associate partners"). Classical theologians, including al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī, and Ibn Kathīr, clarify that the Prophet was divinely protected (*maʿṣūm*) from ever committing idolatry; the hypothetical conditional (*law* or *in*) is employed rhetorically to establish the absolute gravity of the principle. If the greatest and most beloved of creation would face the total annihilation of his deeds were he to compromise monotheism, then how could any lesser mortal imagine themselves exempt?

**The Total Annihilation of Righteous Deeds**

The consequence of polytheism is articulated through the vivid verb *la-yaḥbaṭanna ʿamaluk* ("your deeds will certainly be void"). The root *ḥ-b-ṭ* in classical Arabic was originally used in veterinary pathology to describe an animal that grazes upon poisonous weeds, causing its stomach to swell until its internal organs burst and it dies. In theological semantics, *iḥbāṭ al-ʿamal* denotes the total invalidation, rot, and complete dissolution of good deeds.

Polytheism (*shirk*) acts as a lethal spiritual poison that instantly corrupts the entire vascular system of faith. A person may spend decades building hospitals, feeding millions of orphans, maintaining continuous fasts, and performing extraordinary acts of civic benevolence. Yet if those deeds are offered to an idol, performed for self-deification, or mingled with the worship of created intermediaries, their spiritual value before God is absolute zero. In Sūrah al-Furqān, the Qur'an depicts this tragic eschatological bankruptcy: *“And We will approach what they have done of deeds and make them as scattered dust”* (25:23).

**The Theological Necessity of Pure Intention**

The necessity of monotheism as the sole foundation for the acceptance of deeds is grounded in the foundational requirement of intention (*al-niyyah*). As the Prophet ﷺ famously declared: *“Deeds are judged only by intentions, and every person will have only what they intended”* (*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 1*). Worship is an act of spiritual homage paid to the uncreated Sovereign who bestowed existence, life, and faculties upon the servant.

When a person directs worship or ultimate gratitude to a created intermediary, they commit an act of cosmic treason. They take the energy, breath, and intellect gifted by the Creator and employ them in homage to a creature. In a profound *ḥadīth qudsī*, God declares: *“I am the most self-sufficient, standing in no need of partners. Whoever performs a deed wherein he associates a partner with Me, I abandon him and his partnership”* (*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2985*). Good deeds cannot survive in a contaminated vessel.

**The Inevitable Descent into Ultimate Loss**

The verse concludes with an emphatic confirmation of ruin: *wa-la-takūnanna mina al-khāsirīn* ("and you will truly be one of the losers"). The double emphasis—the prefix *lām* and the energetic *nūn* of intensification—seals the verdict. The individual who commits *shirk* forfeits their earthly exertion, their moral legacy, and their eternal salvation.

In Sūrah al-Anʿām, after enumerating eighteen major prophets—including Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, David, Solomon, Moses, and Jesus—the Qur'an pronounces this identical universal principle: *“That is the guidance of Allah by which He guides whomever He wills of His servants. But if they had associated others with Allah, of no avail to them would be that which they used to do”* (6:88). The law of *iḥbāṭ* is absolute; it admits no personal favoritism, family connections, or historical dispensations.

**Dismantling Moral Self-Righteousness**

Verse 39:65 delivers a profound corrective to secular and religious self-righteousness. Many people cultivate the dangerous assumption that their outward humanitarian deeds or civic contributions guarantee salvation, regardless of their theological convictions. They imagine God as an indifferent accountant who measures raw productivity without regard to whom the homage was directed.

The verse shatters this delusion. Morality cannot be divorced from theology. The foremost moral duty incumbent upon any rational creature is to recognize its Creator and render exclusive gratitude to the Source of all blessings. To live a life of philanthropy while denying the Sustainer who provided the wealth and life is the height of moral perversion. *Tawḥīd* is the foundation upon which the edifice of righteousness is built; without the foundation, the entire structure collapses into ruins.

**The Absolute Urgency of Protecting Faith**

Understanding the fatal nature of *shirk* inspires the believer to maintain relentless vigilance over their heart. The Prophet ﷺ warned his Companions that subtle polytheism (*al-shirk al-khafī*)—such as ostentation (*al-riyāʾ*), where one performs worship to be admired by people—is more hidden than the creeping of an ant upon a smooth black stone in the darkness of the night (*al-Muʿjam al-Kabīr 4443*).

He taught the community to seek daily protection through the timeless prayer: *“O Allah, I seek refuge in You from knowingly associating partners with You, and I seek Your forgiveness for that which I do not know”* (*al-Adab al-Mufrad 716, graded ṣaḥīḥ by al-Albānī*). By anchoring the soul in sincere monotheism, the believer ensures that their prayers, sacrifices, living, and dying belong exclusively to the Lord of the worlds, guarding their good deeds against dissolution and securing eternal salvation.
verses.66:
> Rather, worship Allah ˹alone˺ and be one of the grateful

**A Decisive Syntactic Inversion Toward Pure Worship**

Following the grave warning in verse 65 that polytheism instantly invalidates all deeds, the discourse issues a sharp corrective imperative: *bali Allāha fa-ʿbud wa-kun mina al-shākirīn* ("Rather, worship Allah alone and be one of the grateful"). The adversative particle *bal* ("rather", "nay") abruptly severs all connection with the idolatrous proposals of verse 64 and the ruinous path of verse 65, establishing the single, non-negotiable alternative.

In classical Arabic rhetoric, the syntactic structure of this clause is extraordinarily concentrated. The direct object *Allāh* is fronted before the imperative verb *fa-ʿbud* ("so worship!"), separated by the conjunction *fa*. This grammatical inversion creates absolute restriction and exclusivity (*ḥaṣr wa-ikhtiṣāṣ*): worship God alone, and direct not a single heartbeat, prayer, or sacrifice to any entity besides Him. The imperative *fa-ʿbud* is an immediate practical command that translates theological conviction into active, exclusive servitude, establishing an unshakeable boundary against compromise.

**Gratitude as the Essence of Monotheistic Servitude**

The companion command unites worship with its internal soul: *wa-kun mina al-shākirīn* ("and be one of the grateful"). The root *sh-k-r* denotes recognizing benefit, acknowledging the benefactor, and utilizing the bestowed blessing in the service of its Giver. In the Qur'anic framework, gratitude (*al-shukr*) is not merely a verbal formula muttered after a meal; it is the comprehensive spiritual orientation that stands at the opposite pole of disbelief (*al-kufr*).

In Arabic etymology, *kufr* literally means to cover, conceal, and bury—hence a farmer is called a *kāfir* because he buries a seed in the soil. Applied to theology, the denier (*al-kāfir*) is an ingrate who covers over the radiant blessings of God, attributing His gifts to idols, human ingenuity (*39:49*), or blind nature. In contrast, the grateful person (*al-shākir*) brings the divine origin of all blessings into the light, consecrating their faculties, wealth, and life to the One who bestowed them. To be among the grateful is to be a true monotheist.

**The Inexhaustible Debt of Divine Favor**

The command to be among the grateful is grounded in the staggering reality of divine providence detailed across Sūrah az-Zumar. God created the cosmos in truth (*39:5*), sculpted the human embryo in threefold darkness (*39:6*), provided grazing livestock for civilizational survival (*39:6*), channels rain through underground springs to nourish botanical life (*39:21*), reclaims and returns the soul every night during sleep (*39:42*), and holds the keys to all celestial and terrestrial treasuries (*39:63*).

How could an intelligent human being enjoy these infinite, unearned gifts and then bow down before an inanimate stone statue that provided nothing? Polytheism is the supreme act of ingratitude. By commanding the Prophet—and through him, all humanity—to be among the grateful, the verse reveals that monotheistic worship is the only rational, honorable response to the unceasing river of divine benevolence.

**Enrolling in the Select Fellowship of Shukr**

The phrasing *wa-kun mina al-shākirīn* ("and be among the grateful") employs the plural collective noun, inviting the believer to join a rare and noble spiritual fellowship. Across the Qur'an, scripture notes that while all human beings consume divine blessings, very few cultivate authentic gratitude. Sūrah Sabaʾ laments: *“And few of My servants are grateful”* (34:13).

To be counted among the *shākirīn* is to step out of the herd of entitled consumers and enter the company of the prophets. When the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ stood in nocturnal prayer until his feet cracked and swelled, his beloved wife ʿĀʾishah asked: *“Why do you do this, O Messenger of Allah, when your past and future sins have been forgiven?”* He replied with timeless simplicity: *“Shall I not be a grateful servant?”* (*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4837*). Worship is not a transaction performed out of fear of punishment or desire for reward alone; at its highest station, it is the ecstatic overflow of pure gratitude.

**The Three Dimensions of Authentic Gratitude**

Classical scholars of spiritual purification, such as Ibn al-Qayyim and al-Ghazālī, outline three interrelated dimensions of authentic *shukr*: gratitude of the heart (*al-qalb*), gratitude of the tongue (*al-lisān*), and gratitude of the limbs (*al-jawāriḥ*). Gratitude of the heart is the inward acknowledgment that every blessing originates with God alone. Gratitude of the tongue is praising God, speaking truth, and refraining from complaint.

Gratitude of the limbs is the active utilization of God's gifts in accordance with His pleasure: using physical health to stand in prayer, using wealth to feed the hungry, using intellect to study sacred truth, and using influence to defend the oppressed. If a person claims to be grateful with their tongue while using their wealth to oppress the weak, their claim is a hollow lie. Verse 39:66 demands the complete harmony of all three dimensions in exclusive devotion to the Creator, ensuring that faith permeates every aspect of daily conduct.

**The Indestructible Fortress of Joyful Faith**

Living as one of the grateful transforms the human experience of life. In a world saturated with consumerist anxiety, entitlement, and bitter discontent, the grateful servant discovers an inexhaustible spring of peace. They do not obsess over what they lack; they celebrate the infinite blessings they have already received.

When ease arrives, they respond with humble thanksgiving; when trials descend, they respond with patient endurance, knowing that God's wisdom governs all circumstances (*39:52*). Sincere gratitude preserves existing blessings from decay and attracts divine increase: *“If you are grateful, I will surely increase you”* (14:7). By uniting uncompromised worship with joyful gratitude, verse 39:66 provides the ultimate prescription for spiritual health, liberating the soul from the poisons of pride and leading it into eternal felicity. The grateful servant discovers that devotion is not a heavy burden, but the supreme joy of an awakened life. In that sacred posture, the soul tastes the sweetness of faith every day.
verses.67:
> They have not shown Allah His proper reverence—when on the Day of Judgment the ˹whole˺ earth will be in His Grip, and the heavens will be rolled up in His Right Hand. Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate ˹with Him˺

**The Radical Failure of Cognitive Estimation**

The discourse diagnoses the root intellectual failure underpinning all polytheism and moral rebellion: *wa-mā qadarū Allāha ḥaqqa qadrih* ("They have not shown Allah His proper reverence / they have not estimated Allah with His true measure"). The verb *qadara* signifies measuring, assessing, evaluating, estimating capacity, and recognizing true worth. The cognate accusative *ḥaqqa qadrih* ("the true measure of His worth") indicates the absolute, objective standard of divine majesty.

The polytheists did not necessarily deny God's existence; they acknowledged Him as the ultimate Creator (*39:38*). Their fatal intellectual crime was a catastrophic failure of estimation. They imagined God as an enlarged human king who needs courtiers, shares power with tribal idols, accepts bribes, and remains indifferent to human injustice. To project human limitations, finite biology, and political compromises onto the uncreated Sovereign is to fail completely in grasping who God is. The verse indicts human arrogance for attempting to measure the infinite Creator with the tiny, distorted ruler of creaturely imagination.

**The Eschatological Gripping of the Cosmos**

To correct this pathetic, shrunken estimation of God, the verse unveils an overwhelming cosmological vision of the Day of Resurrection: *wa-l-arḍu jamīʿan qabḍatuhu yawma al-qiyāmati wa-l-samāwātu maṭwiyyātun bi-yamīnih* ("when on the Day of Judgment the whole earth will be in His Grip, and the heavens will be rolled up in His Right Hand"). The noun *qabḍah* denotes a single handful, a fistful, or an effortless grasp.

The entire physical planet—its towering mountain ranges, continental landmasses, deepest ocean trenches, and billions of inhabitants—will be nothing more than a tiny particle held effortlessly in the divine grasp. Simultaneously, the vast celestial heavens—with their billions of galaxies, expanding cosmic voids, and stellar clusters—will be rolled up like a parchment scroll (*maṭwiyyāt*) in His right hand (*21:104*). The imagery conveys infinite, effortless omnipotence. The entire physical universe that dazzles human senses is completely dwarfed before the uncreated majesty of the Lord.

**The Rabbinic Interlocutor and Prophetic Vindication**

Classical exegetes, including al-Bukhārī, Muslim, al-Ṭabarī, and Ibn Kathīr, record the famous historical encounter connected with this revelation. ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd narrated that a Jewish scholar (a rabbi) came to the Messenger of God ﷺ and said: *“O Muḥammad, we find in our scriptures that Allah will place the heavens on one finger, the earths on one finger, the trees on one finger, the water and the dust on one finger, and all the rest of creation on one finger; then He will shake them and say: ‘I am the King! Where are the kings of the earth?’”*

Upon hearing this description of divine majesty, the Messenger of God ﷺ smiled broadly until his molar teeth were visible, confirming the truth of the rabbi's statement, and then recited this very verse: *“They have not shown Allah His proper reverence—when on the Day of Judgment the whole earth will be in His Grip, and the heavens will be rolled up in His Right Hand”* (39:67; *Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4811; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2786*). The narration demonstrates that authentic monotheistic revelation across all prophetic traditions shares this sublime, awe-inspiring vision of absolute divine transcendence.

**The Classical Hermeneutics of Divine Attributes**

The mention of the "Grip" (*al-qabḍah*) and the "Right Hand" (*al-yamīn*) represents a foundational locus in classical Islamic theology (*al-asmāʾ wa-l-ṣifāt*). Sunni scholarship approached these descriptions through two complementary, orthodox methodologies, both rigorously upholding divine transcendence.

The early authorities (*al-salaf*) affirmed these attributes as literal textual realities suited to divine majesty without asking "how" (*bi-lā kayf*), without anthropomorphic comparison (*bi-lā tamthīl*), and without nullification (*bi-l-tʿṭīl*), adhering strictly to the principle: *“There is nothing like unto Him, and He is the All-Hearing, All-Seeing”* (42:11). Later theologians (*al-khalaf*) explained them as sublime allegorical expressions (*kināyah*) denoting absolute power, unrestricted sovereignty, and effortless cosmic domination. Under both interpretive frameworks, the theological conclusion is identical: God is completely free from physical limbs, spatial containment, or creaturely form.

**The Burst of Absolute Transcendence**

The verse culminates in an ecstatic declaration of cosmic purification: *subḥānahu wa-taʿālā ʿammā yushrikūn* ("Glorified and Exalted is He above what they associate with Him!"). The verbal noun *subḥān* denotes declaring God absolutely distant and free from every deficiency, partner, child, or limitation (*39:4*). The companion verb *taʿālā* asserts supreme, unassailable elevation above all created realities.

The contrast drawn across the verse is breathtaking. On one side stands the Almighty, who holds the planetary globe in His grip and rolls up the galaxies like a scroll; on the other side stand the pathetic idols and fabricated patrons of polytheism. How could any sane intellect place a carved stone, an angel, a prophet, or a worldly ideology alongside the One who folds up the universe? The exclamation *subḥānahu wa-taʿālā* clears the consciousness of all idolatrous dust, restoring the solitary glory of the Creator.

**The Awakening of Awe and True Worship**

Verse 39:67 is designed to produce a profound spiritual earthquake within the human soul. When an individual contemplates the earth as a handful in the divine grasp, human pride collapses. The proud emperors who built monuments, the tyrannical regimes that oppressed nations, and the wealthy elites who strutted in vanity are revealed as microscopic dust specks living upon a grain of sand.

Estimating God with His true measure (*ḥaqqa qadrih*) is the beginning of authentic wisdom. When a servant grasps even a glimpse of this divine majesty, worship ceases to be a routine chore. Prayer becomes an awe-inspiring standing before the King of the universe; repentance becomes an urgent plea for shelter; and gratitude becomes the defining breath of life. The soul is freed from fear of mortals, anchored in reverence for the Sovereign who holds the cosmos in His hand.
verses.68:
> The Trumpet will be blown and all those in the heavens and all those on the earth will fall dead, except those Allah wills ˹to spare˺. Then it will be blown again and they will rise up at once, looking on ˹in anticipation˺

**The Apocalyptic Blast of Universal Annihilation**

The discourse transitions from the sublime majesty of the Creator holding the cosmos to the apocalyptic reality that initiates the Hereafter: *wa-nufikha fī al-ṣūri fa-ṣaʿiqa man fī al-samāwāti wa-man fī al-arḍi illā man shāʾa Allāh* ("The Trumpet will be blown and all those in the heavens and all those on the earth will fall dead, except those Allah wills to spare"). The passive construction *wa-nufikha* ("and it will be blown") conveys solemn, inexorable inevitability. The instrument is *al-ṣūr*—the great celestial Horn entrusted to the Archangel Isrāfīl, who stands poised with his lips upon the mouthpiece, his gaze fixed upon the divine Throne, awaiting the sovereign command.

The verb *ṣaʿiqa* derives from *al-ṣāʿiqah*, denoting thunderous striking, swooning, fainting, and collapsing dead from sheer auditory and metaphysical shock. It is the first of two apocalyptic trumpet blasts: the Blast of Stupefaction and Annihilation (*nafkhat al-ṣaʿq*). The shockwave of this celestial sound shatters the physical laws of the universe. In a single terrifying fraction of a second, every living consciousness across celestial galaxies and terrestrial lands—human beings, jinn, beasts, and angels—falls lifeless.

**The Divine Exemption from the First Blast**

The text introduces a profound theological exception: *illā man shāʾa Allāh* ("except those Allah wills to spare"). Classical commentators, including al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and Ibn Kathīr, explore the identity of those spared from the initial blast. Foremost among them are the highest angelic hierarchy: the four Archangels—Jibrīl, Mīkāʾīl, Isrāfīl, and the Angel of Death (ʿIzrāʾīl)—as well as the bearers of the divine Throne (*ḥamalat al-ʿarsh*).

According to verified eschatological traditions, these supreme beings will remain alive until God commands the Angel of Death to claim their souls one by one, until only the Angel of Death remains. God then commands him to die, leaving only the uncreated, Ever-Living Sovereign alone in existence, proclaiming across the cosmic silence: *“To whom belongs sovereignty this Day? To Allah, the One, the Prevailing!”* (40:16). Other classical opinions include the martyrs (*al-shuhadāʾ*), who are already alive with their Lord receiving provision (*3:169*), and the maidens and attendants of Paradise.

**The Second Blast: The Universal Awakening**

The narrative pivots to the miraculous reversal of mortality: *thumma nufikha fīhi ukhrā fa-idhā hum qiyāmun yanẓurūn* ("Then it will be blown again and they will rise up at once, looking on in anticipation"). The conjunction *thumma* marks an interval between the two cosmic events. The Prophet ﷺ was asked about the duration between the two blasts, and he replied: *“Forty.”* The narrator Abū Hurayrah was asked whether it meant forty days, forty months, or forty years, but he declined to speculate, affirming only the number forty (*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4935; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2955*).

During this cosmic pause, God sends down a celestial rain resembling dew, from which human bodies sprout from the earth like vegetation, reassembled from their indestructible tailbone (*ʿajb al-dhanab*). Then the Archangel Isrāfīl is resurrected to blow the second blast: the Blast of Resurrection (*nafkhat al-baʿth wa-l-nushūr*). Instantly, billions of souls reunite with their perfected bodies, bursting forth from the dust in throngs (*78:18*).

**The Posture of Sudden Awakening and Anticipation**

The verse captures the instantaneous nature of the resurrection through the surprise particle *idhā al-fujāʾiyyah*: *fa-idhā hum qiyāmun yanẓurūn* ("and, behold, they are standing, looking on!"). There is no groggy convalescence, no slow rehabilitation, and no medical recovery. In the blink of an eye, every human being who ever walked the earth stands upright upon their feet (*qiyām*).

The active participle *yanẓurūn* ("looking on") conveys profound psychological bewilderment, shock, and acute anticipation. Their eyes dart across the transformed landscape of the plains of reckoning (*14:48*), beholding the unfurled skies, the arriving angels, and the terrifying majesty of the divine judgment seat. The deniers cry out in absolute horror: *“Woe to us! Who has raised us up from our sleeping place? This is what the Most Merciful had promised, and the messengers told the truth!”* (36:52). The debate is over; the unseen has become terrifyingly visible.

**A Direct Vindication of the Physical Resurrection**

Verse 39:68 stands as an irrefutable answer to ancient and modern skepticism regarding the bodily resurrection. The pagan Arabs repeatedly mocked the Prophet's proclamation of the Last Day, asking: *“When we are dead and become dust and bones, will we indeed be resurrected?”* (56:47).

The verse demonstrates that resurrecting billions of human beings does not require complex technological labor or prolonged exertion for the Almighty. It requires merely two celestial trumpet blasts. The first sound ends all mortal life; the second sound restores all conscious existence. In Sūrah al-Qamar, the Qur'an emphasizes this effortless power: *“And Our command is but one, like the glancing of an eye”* (54:50). The One who created the vast cosmos with a single word (*kun*) restores humanity with equal ease.

**The Call to Prepare for the Awakening**

Contemplating the trumpet blast transforms an individual's orientation toward mortal life. The day will arrive when the noise of worldly business, political conflict, and domestic concerns will be permanently silenced by the celestial blast. The only question that matters is: in what state will you rise when the second trumpet sounds?

The Prophet ﷺ warned that people will be resurrected in the exact state upon which they died: *“Every servant will be resurrected upon that which he died”* (*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2878*). The one who dies in sincere prostration will rise prostrating; the one who dies in repentance will rise with light; and the one who dies in arrogant denial will rise with blackened features (*39:60*). By maintaining mindful awareness of the Trumpet today, the believer lives in continuous moral readiness, ensuring that their awakening will be a moment of joyous redemption rather than terrifying despair.
verses.69:
> The earth will shine with the light of its Lord, the record ˹of deeds˺ will be laid ˹open˺, the prophets and the witnesses will be brought forward—and judgment will be passed on all with fairness. None will be wronged

**The Luminous Transformation of the Plain of Gathering**

The discourse presents the majestic inauguration of the supreme cosmic courtroom: *wa-ashraqati al-arḍu bi-nūri rabbihā* ("The earth will shine with the light of its Lord"). The verb *ashraqat* denotes radiant illumination, sunrise, and the bursting forth of brilliant, unshadowed light. The plain of gathering (*arḍ al-maḥshar*) is not the current geographical earth; it is a transfigured landscape described in Sūrah Ibrāhīm: *“On the Day the earth will be replaced by another earth, and the heavens as well”* (14:48).

It is a vast, leveled, pristine white plain without mountains, valleys, landmarks, or hiding places (*20:106–107*). On that Day, the sun, moon, and stars are extinguished (*81:1–2*); the plain is illuminated exclusively by the uncreated, transcendent majesty and justice of God as He descends in a manner befitting His glory to judge His creation (*89:22*). In that pure divine light, all spiritual darkness, falsehood, and deception are dissolved; every hidden motive and secret thought is exposed before the eyes of all creation.

**The Deposition of the Indelible Records**

The second judicial proceeding is the presentation of evidence: *wa-wuḍiʿa al-kitāb* ("the record of deeds will be laid open"). The singular noun *al-kitāb* operates collectively, referring both to the universal master record (*al-lawḥ al-maḥfūẓ*) and to the individual scrolls of deeds recorded by the noble guardian angels (*al-kirām al-kātibīn*, 82:10–12).

The passive verb *wuḍiʿa* ("will be placed", "laid down") signifies the official opening of the evidentiary archives. The scrolls will be unrolled and placed in the hands of their owners: the righteous receiving them in their right hands with joyful exclamation (*69:19*), and the wicked receiving them in their left hands behind their backs with cries of ruin (*69:25; 84:10*). In Sūrah al-Kahf, the sinners look at this meticulous archive in absolute terror: *“And the record will be placed, and you will see the criminals fearful of that which is in it, and they will say: ‘Oh, woe to us! What is this book that leaves nothing small or great except that it has enumerated it?’”* (18:49). Every stolen coin, every whispered lie, and every act of compassion is recorded without omission.

**The Assembly of Prophets and Witnesses**

The courtroom then convenes the witness tier: *wa-jīʾa bi-l-nabiyyīna wa-l-shuhadāʾ* ("the prophets and the witnesses will be brought forward"). The prophets are summoned first to bear formal legal testimony regarding their missions: they will testify that they faithfully delivered the divine message, warned their peoples, and commanded uncompromised monotheism (*5:109; 7:6*).

Alongside the prophets stand *al-shuhadāʾ*—the witnesses. Classical commentators, including al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, and Ibn Kathīr, examine the multifaceted categories of witnesses. They include the guardian angels who recorded human deeds; the righteous martyrs who testified to truth with their blood; the community of Muḥammad ﷺ, which will bear witness that past prophets delivered their messages (*2:143*); and the very physical faculties and earth itself, which will speak and testify to the actions performed upon them (*41:20–21; 99:4*). The evidence is multiple, corroborative, and unimpeachable.

**The Flawless Execution of Impartial Justice**

The verdict is announced with absolute legal majesty: *wa-quḍiya baynahum bi-l-ḥaqqi wa-hum lā yuẓlamūn* ("and judgment will be passed on all with fairness. None will be wronged"). The verb *quḍiya* signifies final, binding, and unalterable judicial determination. The adverbial phrase *bi-l-ḥaqq* ("with truth", "with absolute fairness") establishes that the judgment is grounded in objective reality and perfect equity.

The concluding guarantee—*wa-hum lā yuẓlamūn* ("and they will not be wronged")—is the foundational constitutional principle of Qur'anic theodicy. Not a single soul will have an evil deed added to their record that they did not commit; not a single righteous deed will be minimized or overlooked; and not a single punishment will exceed the measure of guilt. In Sūrah al-Anbiyāʾ, God reaffirms this flawless precision: *“And We place the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, so no soul will be treated unjustly at all. And if there is even the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth”* (21:47). Justice is executed with microscopic perfection.

**The Radical Inversion of Earthly Courts**

Verse 39:69 stands in dramatic contrast to the corrupt, biased courtrooms of human history. In earthly tribunals, wealth purchases elite defense attorneys, political tyranny silences witnesses, evidence is fabricated, and the poor and vulnerable are routinely crushed by institutional injustice.

In the celestial courtroom of the Almighty, all worldly advantages evaporate. Emperors and slaves stand naked, barefoot, and uncircumcised upon the identical plain of gathering (*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6527*). Bribes are impossible, perjury is eradicated, and human connections provide zero influence (*39:44*). The Judge is the All-Knowing Creator who witnessed every deed in real time. For the victims of earthly oppression, this verse is the ultimate guarantee of historical vindication; for the arrogant oppressors, it is the death knell of all impunity.

**Preparing for the Supreme Evidentiary Opening**

Contemplating the day when the Book is laid open and the prophets stand as witnesses inspires immediate moral sobriety. Every human being is currently authoring the very scroll that will be read aloud before the gathered assembly of humanity, jinn, and angels. The words you speak today, the business transactions you execute, and the private thoughts you harbor are being inked into an indestructible record.

The wise believer acts with continuous vigilance, ensuring that their daily writing reflects faith, compassion, and justice. When an error is committed, they rush to erase it immediately through sincere repentance and good deeds, knowing that *“good deeds wipe out evil deeds”* (11:114). By aligning one's life with revealed truth today, the soul prepares to stand before the light of its Lord in joyous confidence, ready to receive its record in the right hand and enter the everlasting peace of the righteous.
verses.70:
> Every soul will be paid in full for its deeds, for Allah knows best what they have done

**The Absolute Mathematical Settlement of Deeds**

The judicial proceedings outlined in verse 69 reach their precise economic and moral conclusion: *wa-wuffiyat kullu nafsin mā ʿamilat* ("Every soul will be paid in full for its deeds"). The verb *wuffiyat* derives from *al-wafāʾ*, meaning to pay in full, complete an exact transaction, settle a debt without leaving the slightest fraction unpaid, and deliver complete compensation. The passive construction emphasizes the objective certainty of the law: the payout is guaranteed by divine decree.

The universal quantifier *kullu nafs* ("every soul") encompasses all human beings without exception: kings, prophets, slaves, billionaires, and destitutes. The phrase *mā ʿamilat* ("what it did") establishes that the currency of the Hereafter is strictly moral action. In this mortal life, people are frequently compensated unfairly: workers are exploited, corrupt executives hoard unearned wealth, and righteous laborers are overlooked. On the Day of Resurrection, all distorted balances are corrected. Every single soul receives the full, unmitigated payout of its own choices, without deduction or delay.

**The Omniscient Foundation of Divine Recompense**

The second clause articulates the epistemic guarantee that underpins this perfect payout: *wa-huwa aʿlamu bi-mā yafʿalūn* ("for Allah knows best what they have done"). The superlative form *aʿlam* ("knows best", "possesses absolute, supreme knowledge") establishes that divine compensation does not rely upon the testimony of fallible human witnesses, nor does it depend upon physical records to inform God.

God was the direct, living Witness to every deed at the exact moment of its execution. He knew the hidden intention (*al-niyyah*) that stirred in the heart before the limb moved, the private temptation that was resisted in the dark, and the secret duplicity concealed beneath a pious smile. The witness tier and written books described in verse 69 exist not to inform the Almighty, but to establish incontrovertible legal proof before the creature, leaving the sinner without a shred of denial or excuse. Divine knowledge encompasses all hidden dimensions.

**The Radical Symmetry of Grace and Equity**

Classical theologians, including al-Bayḍāwī, al-Zamakhsharī, and al-Rāzī, examine the profound theological synthesis between *al-wafāʾ* (full payment) and divine grace (*al-faḍl*). When an evil deed is paid in full, it is compensated with exact, unmagnified justice: one sin receives exactly one measure of punishment (*6:160*), and God often pardons through repentance and expiation (*39:35; 39:53*).

However, when a righteous deed is paid in full, divine generosity multiplies the payout far beyond the value of human exertion. A single sincere action is rewarded tenfold, seventy-fold, or seven hundred-fold, culminating in the boundless recompense of the patient (*39:10*). Paying the soul in full (*wuffiyat*) therefore means that the scale of justice is never tipped against the servant; the wrongdoer receives strictly what they earned, while the believer receives their full earnings multiplied by infinite divine bounty.

**The Contrast With Worldly Injustice and Exploitation**

Verse 39:70 provides profound psychological consolation to all who have suffered injustice, oppression, and exploitation throughout human history. Countless martyrs have died in dark dungeons without seeing justice; countless laborers have spent their lives in exhausting toil only to die in poverty; and countless tyrants have lived lavish lives and died peacefully in bed without facing earthly accountability.

If this mortal world were the only arena of existence, human history would be an unbearable tragedy of meaningless suffering and unrectified grief. Verse 39:70 proclaims that the final ledger has not yet been closed. Earthly life was merely the day of work (*yawm al-ʿamal*); the Day of Resurrection is the day of absolute payday (*yawm al-jazāʾ*). No tear shed in patience is forgotten, no sacrifice made for truth is lost, and no act of tyranny escapes unpunished. Every account will be balanced to the last atom with majestic perfection.

**The Shift From Individual Accountability to Collective Sorting**

Verse 70 marks the definitive closing of the courtroom phase of Sūrah az-Zumar. Across verses 68 through 70, the text surveyed the apocalyptic trumpet blasts, the resurrection of bodies, the illumination of the earth, the deposition of the scrolls, the testimony of witnesses, and the final payout of deeds. Every soul has been examined, evaluated, and given its individual verdict.

This exhaustive individual accounting prepares the way for the grand climax of the chapter: the collective driving of humanity into its two eternal destinations. The sūrah will now transition from individual trial to cosmic segregation: the driving of the disbelievers in throngs (*zumar*) toward the gates of Hell (vv. 71–72), and the leading of the reverent in throngs (*zumar*) toward the open gates of Paradise (vv. 73–74). The individual payout of verse 70 determines the eternal company of verse 71.

**Living With the Consciousness of the Full Payment**

Contemplating the reality of *wuffiyat kullu nafs* reshapes an individual's daily economic and moral priorities. When a person realizes that every action is a deposit in an eternal account, they cease to be obsessed with immediate worldly returns. They do not lose heart when righteous deeds go unacknowledged by fellow mortals, nor do they despair when virtue goes unrewarded in the marketplace.

The believer works for an Employer whose knowledge is absolute and whose treasuries are inexhaustible (*39:63*). One is inspired to invest generously in acts of hidden charity, upright speech, and patient service, knowing that every atom of goodness will be returned in full on the Day of Account. Living with this awareness fills the soul with deep dignity, freeing it from the need for human validation and anchoring its hopes in the flawless justice of the Lord of the worlds. In that certainty, the believer finds enduring purpose, walking through mortal life with steady, confident steps. That unshakeable trust transforms every mundane effort into an act of eternal devotion.
verses.71:
> Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in ˹successive˺ groups. When they arrive there, its gates will be opened and its keepers will ask them: “Did messengers not come to you from among yourselves, reciting to you the revelations of your Lord and warning you of the coming of this Day of yours?” The disbelievers will cry, “Yes ˹indeed˺! But the decree of torment has come to pass against the disbelievers.”

**The Violent Herding Toward the Abyss**

Following the universal settlement of deeds in verse 70, the sūrah reaches the grand eschatological scene from which it derives its title: *wa-sīqa alladhīna kafarū ilā jahannama zumarā* ("Those who disbelieved will be driven to Hell in successive groups"). The verb *sīqa* is the passive of *sāqa*, meaning to drive cattle, herd animals with sticks, or violently force recalcitrant prisoners forward against their will.

In this life, the arrogant walked upon the earth with boastful autonomy, rejecting divine guidance and mocking the warnings of the prophets. On the Day of Judgment, that illusion of autonomy is stripped away. They do not walk willingly; they are dragged, shoved, and forcibly herded toward the blazing abyss by stern angelic wardens (*52:13*). The noun *zumarā* (the plural of *zumrah*) signifies distinct crowds, cohorts, factions, or successive throngs. The commentators explain that they are segregated into ideological groups: tyrants with tyrants, idolaters with idolaters, corrupt hypocrites with corrupt hypocrites, each cohort categorized according to the specific nature and degree of their earthly crimes.

**The Abrupt Opening of the Seven Gates**

The narrative details the grim arrival: *ḥattā idhā jāʾūhā futiḥat abwābuhā* ("When they arrive there, its gates will be opened"). In Arabic grammar, the past tense *futiḥat* ("were flung open") occurs without the conjunction *wāw*, indicating sudden, terrifying immediacy. The gates of Hell remain tightly locked until the wretched throngs reach the threshold; then, as they arrive in terror, the colossal iron gates are violently thrown open before them.

The sudden unbolting exposes the roaring inferno within, blasting the condemned with unbearable heat, suffocating fumes, and deafening shrieks (*67:7*). Classical commentators contrast this with verse 73, where the gates of Paradise are already standing open before the arrival of the righteous (*wa-futiḥat abwābuhā*). For the deniers, the abrupt unsealing of the gates represents the sudden, inescapable snapping of a cosmic trap, sealing them off permanently from light and hope.

**The Interrogation by the Angelic Wardens**

At the threshold of destruction, the angelic wardens—the nineteen stern keepers of Hell (*al-zabāniyah*, 74:30)—confront the condemned with an agonizing judicial interrogation: *a-lam yaʾtikum rusulun minkum yatlūna ʿalaykum āyāti rabbikum wa-yundhirūnakum liqāʾa yawmikum hādhā* ("Did messengers not come to you from among yourselves, reciting to you the revelations of your Lord and warning you of the coming of this Day of yours?").

This interrogation (*istifhām al-tawbīkh wa-l-tabkīt*) is designed not to gather information, but to deepen psychological anguish and force a public confession of guilt. The keepers remind them of the perfection of divine justice: God did not leave humanity in ignorance, nor did He dispatch incomprehensible alien beings. He sent human messengers (*rusulun minkum*) who spoke their language, lived among them, and recited clear revealed verses. Furthermore, they were repeatedly warned about this specific Day (*liqāʾa yawmikum hādhā*). The condemned had every intellectual and moral opportunity to turn back, repent, and seek divine mercy (*39:53*).

**The Tragic Confession of Guilt**

Confronted with the irrefutable truth, the disbelievers offer an immediate, broken admission: *qālū balā wa-lākin ḥaqqat kalimatu al-ʿadhābi ʿalā al-kāfirīn* ("The disbelievers will cry, 'Yes indeed! But the decree of torment has come to pass against the disbelievers'"). The affirmative particle *balā* shatters all remaining defense: yes, indeed, the messengers came, the verses were recited, and the warnings were delivered.

Their subsequent lament—*wa-lākin ḥaqqat kalimatu al-ʿadhāb* ("but the decree of torment has come to pass")—is not an evasion of personal responsibility, but a despairing realization of the unalterable divine law. In Sūrah al-Mulk, the Qur'an captures their bitter self-recrimination: *“And they will say: ‘If only we had been listening or reasoning, we would not be among the companions of the Blaze.’ So they will confess their sin, so away with the companions of the Blaze!”* (67:10–11). They realize too late that their damnation was not an arbitrary divine decree, but the inevitable harvest of their own stubborn denial.

**The Complete Vindication of Divine Justice**

Verse 39:71 establishes the absolute equity of Qur'anic eschatology. No human being is cast into Hell without having received clear warning and prophetic guidance during their earthly life. In Sūrah al-Isrāʾ, God proclaims: *“And never would We punish until We sent a messenger”* (17:15).

Damnation is preceded by multiple layers of proof: the cosmic signs in nature (*39:5*), the internal testimonies of the soul (*39:42*), the recitation of scripture (*39:23*), the historical warnings of past civilizations (*39:25*), and the compassionate summons to repentance (*39:53*). When the condemned confess *balā* ("Yes indeed"), they absolve the Creator of all injustice and take full ownership of their self-inflicted ruin. Divine judgment is proven universally righteous and beyond reproach.

**Heeding the Warnings Before the Threshold**

Contemplating the terrifying arrival at the gates of Hell awakens the human heart from spiritual complacency. Today, we are still living in the earthly realm where the revelations of our Lord are recited, the messengers' teachings are accessible, and the door of repentance remains wide open. The interrogation of verse 71 has not yet been addressed to us.

The wise believer reads this verse as an urgent summons to moral accountability. One does not wait until the iron gates of Hell swing open to admit the truth. By listening to the warnings today, honoring the messengers, and repenting before the meeting with this Day arrives, the soul escapes the wretched throngs of the condemned and secures a place among those who will be led in honor to the everlasting Garden.
verses.72:
> It will be said to them, “Enter the gates of Hell, to stay there forever.” What an evil home for the arrogant

**The Final Judicial Command of Incarceration**

Following their public confession of guilt at the threshold in verse 71, the definitive sentence of eternal incarceration is executed: *qīla udkhulū abwāba jahannama khālidīna fīhā* ("It will be said to them, 'Enter the gates of Hell, to stay there forever'"). The passive construction *qīla* ("it will be said") reflects supreme sovereign detachment: the sentence is pronounced with chilling, unanswerable finality by divine decree through the angelic wardens.

The imperative *udkhulū* ("enter!") is not an invitation; it is a humiliating command accompanied by violent physical thrusting into the fire (*52:13*). The mention of "gates" in the plural (*abwāba jahannama*) confirms the architectural hierarchy of the inferno. In Sūrah al-Ḥijr, the Qur'an details: *“It has seven gates; for every gate is of them a portion divided”* (15:44). Each sinner enters the specific gate corresponding to the precise nature, weight, and depth of their transgressions, descending into descending levels (*darakāt*) of torment.

**The Horror of Perpetual Confinement**

The condition of entry is defined by the devastating active participle: *khālidīna fīhā* ("abiding therein forever"). In Arabic eschatology, *al-khulūd* denotes permanent, unending duration without interruption, parole, or cessation. The gates through which they enter are permanently locked and bolted behind them: *“Over them is a fire closed in”* (90:20), reinforced with extended pillars (*104:9*).

The psychological terror of Hell is intensified by the absolute impossibility of death or relief. When the damned cry out from within the flames begging for annihilation—*“O Mālik, let your Lord put an end to us!”*—the warden of Hell replies after long epochs: *“Indeed, you will remain”* (43:77). In a well-known authentic narration, the Prophet ﷺ described that death itself will be brought on the Day of Resurrection in the form of a black-and-white ram, placed between Paradise and Hell, and slaughtered. Then a caller will announce: *“O people of Paradise, eternity and no death! O people of Hell, eternity and no death!”* (*Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 4730; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2849*). For the deniers, all hope of reprieve is permanently extinguished.

**Arrogance Identified as the Cardinal Sin**

The verse concludes with an emphatic moral indictment that cuts to the root of human damnation: *fa-biʾsa mathwā al-mutakabbirīn* ("What an evil home for the arrogant!"). The verb of disparagement *biʾsa* expresses absolute revulsion and supreme vilification. The noun *mathwā* denotes a permanent residence, lodging, or settling place.

The text does not identify the inhabitants simply as sinners, criminals, or thieves; it names them *al-mutakabbirīn*—the arrogant. In the moral taxonomy of Sūrah az-Zumar, arrogance (*al-kibr*) is the primal root of all spiritual decay. Earlier in the sūrah, God exposed this inner disease: *“Is there not in Hell a residence for the arrogant?”* (*39:60*). It was arrogance that caused Iblīs to refuse the divine command to prostrate before Adam (*7:12*), and it was arrogance that drove the Meccan chieftains to reject the Prophet Muḥammad ﷺ because he was an orphan rather than an elite nobleman.

**The Psychology and Mechanics of Arrogance**

The Prophet ﷺ provided the definitive psychological definition of arrogance in an authentic tradition: *“Arrogance is rejecting the truth and looking down upon people”* (*baṭar al-ḥaqqi wa-ghamṭu al-nās*, *Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 91*). Arrogance operates on two destructive axes: a vertical rebellion against God and a horizontal contempt for fellow human beings.

On the vertical axis, the arrogant person refuses to submit to divine authority. When clear evidence, logical arguments, and sacred revelations are presented to them, they reject them because accepting truth requires humbling the ego before a higher Sovereign. On the horizontal axis, the arrogant person views themselves as inherently superior to others by virtue of lineage, race, wealth, intelligence, or status. Because they refused to humble their proud necks before their Creator in this world, they are forcibly humbled in the humiliating abasement of Hell. The punishment is tailored with flawless symmetry to the crime.

**The Stark Contrast With the Gates of Paradise**

Verse 39:72 forms the terrifying companion to verse 73, where the gates of Paradise are unlocked for the mindful believers. While the arrogant are commanded *udkhulū abwāba jahannam* with contempt and harshness, the righteous are welcomed with words of peace, love, and celebration: *“Peace be upon you! You have done well, so enter it, to abide forever”* (*39:73*).

While Hell is the residence of the proud (*mathwā al-mutakabbirīn*), Paradise is the home of the humble (*dār al-muttaqīn*). The contrasting destinies illustrate that human destiny is not determined by external material success, but by the internal posture of the heart. The proud soul that exalted itself above truth is cast into the lowest pit, while the humble soul that lowered its forehead to the dust in sincere prostration is raised to the highest chambers of the heavenly realm.

**Purifying the Soul from the Poison of Pride**

The warning of verse 39:72 compels the reflective believer to examine the inner corridors of their soul for any trace of pride. The Prophet ﷺ issued a sobering warning: *“No one who has an atom's weight of arrogance in their heart will enter Paradise”* (*Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 91*). Arrogance is a deceptive spiritual malignancy that can easily mask itself as intellectual sophistication, social standing, or even religious pride.

The remedy for arrogance is continuous self-effacement, intentional service to the vulnerable, and constant remembrance of human origins: a creature sculpted from lowly clay (*32:7*) and sustained entirely by divine mercy (*39:53*). By voluntarily breaking the ego today through humble worship and compassionate conduct, the believer protects their soul from the terrifying sentence of *udkhulū abwāba jahannam* and prepares to receive the angelic greeting of peace at the gates of eternal bliss.
verses.73:
> And those who were mindful of their Lord will be led to Paradise in ˹successive˺ groups. When they arrive at its ˹already˺ open gates, its keepers will say, “Peace be upon you! You have done well, so come in, to stay forever.”

**The Majestic Procession of the God-Fearing**
